items.stem: Which is the correct definition of the term "chiral catalyst"?
options: An equimolar mixture of two enantiomers, which does not rotate plane-polarised light.
A catalyst, often an enzyme or a metal complex with a chiral ligand, that produces mainly one enantiomer.
A pair of optical isomers that are non-superimposable mirror images of each other.
A carbon atom bonded to four different atoms or groups, giving rise to optical isomers.
items.answer: A catalyst, often an enzyme or a metal complex with a chiral ligand, that produces mainly one enantiomer.
items.markingKey: Chiral catalyst: a catalyst, often an enzyme or a metal complex with a chiral ligand, that produces mainly one enantiomer.

items.stem: Nucleophilic addition of HCN to ethanal gives a racemic product because
options: the planar C=O can be attacked equally from either side
the product has no chiral centre
items.answer: the planar C=O can be attacked equally from either side
items.markingKey: Equal chance of each enantiomer.

items.stem: Why can enzymes distinguish between enantiomers?
options: Enzymes destroy one enantiomer by heat
Their active sites are chiral, so only one enantiomer fits and binds correctly
items.answer: Their active sites are chiral, so only one enantiomer fits and binds correctly
items.markingKey: Shape complementarity.

items.stem: How many chiral centres are present in alanine, CH₃CH(NH₂)COOH?
items.markingKey: alanine, CH₃CH(NH₂)COOH: 1 chiral centre(s).

items.stem: State the number of chiral centres in menthol and the maximum number of stereoisomers that could exist because of them.
items.answer: 3 chiral centre(s); maximum 2³ = 8 stereoisomer(s)

items.stem: A pharmaceutical company in Dhaka manufactures L-DOPA, which has 1 chiral centre: only the L-enantiomer is used to treat Parkinson's disease; the D-form has side effects. (a) Explain what is meant by a chiral centre and describe how the two enantiomers differ. (b) Describe two ways the company could obtain the single active enantiomer.
items.answer: (a) A carbon atom attached to four different groups; enantiomers are non-superimposable mirror images that rotate plane-polarised light in opposite directions. (b) Use a chiral catalyst or enzyme (stereoselective synthesis); start from a natural chiral molecule (chiral pool); or resolve the racemate (chiral chromatography / diastereomeric salts).
items.markingKey: (a) definition [1]; mirror images / optical activity [1] [2] (b) any 2 from: Use a chiral catalyst or enzyme (stereoselective synthesis); start from a natural chiral molecule (chiral pool); or resolve the racemate (chiral chromatography / diastereomeric salts) (1 mark each) [2]

items.stem: Which molecule contains a chiral centre?
items.answer: Butan-2-ol
items.markingKey: C2 has H, OH, CH₃ and C₂H₅.

items.stem: Explain why many synthetic reactions produce a racemic mixture.
items.answer: If an intermediate (e.g. a planar carbocation or C=O) is attacked equally from either side, both enantiomers form in equal amounts.
items.markingKey: If an intermediate (e.g. a planar carbocation or C=O) is attacked equally from either side [1]; both enantiomers form in equal amounts [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why it is important for a drug to be produced as a single optical isomer.
items.answer: Receptors in the body are chiral, so the two enantiomers may have different effects: one may be inactive or harmful (e.g. thalidomide); a single isomer allows a smaller dose and fewer side effects, and is required by regulators.
items.markingKey: chiral receptors [1]; different activity / harm [1]; dose / side effects [1] [3]

items.stem: Explain why resolving a racemic mixture is wasteful.
items.answer: At least half of the product is the unwanted enantiomer, which must be discarded or converted, lowering the yield and increasing cost and waste.
items.markingKey: any 2 from: At least half of the product is the unwanted enantiomer; which must be discarded or converted; lowering the yield and increasing cost and waste (1 mark each) [2]

items.stem: Lucas writes in a revision note: "Enantiomers have different chemical properties in all reactions." Identify the error and write a correct statement.
items.answer: Enantiomers have identical chemical properties except in reactions with other chiral molecules (e.g. enzymes, receptors).
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies the error / statement is incorrect; 1 mark: Enantiomers have identical chemical properties except in reactions with other chiral molecules (e.g. enzymes, receptors). [2]

items.answer: 80.0 kg; 60.0% wasted

items.answer: Chiral centre and enantiomers; chiral receptors give different activities; thalidomide example; synthetic routes often give racemates (planar intermediates); methods: resolution (wasteful, ≤50%), chiral catalysts/enzymes (stereoselective), chiral pool starting materials (amino acids, sugars); advantages: smaller dose, fewer side effects; disadvantages: cost, extra steps; evaluation.

items.stem: A pharmaceutical company in Seoul manufactures L-DOPA, which has 1 chiral centre: only the L-enantiomer is used to treat Parkinson's disease; the D-form has side effects. (c) Describe two ways the company could obtain the single active enantiomer.
items.answer: (a) A carbon atom attached to four different groups; enantiomers are non-superimposable mirror images that rotate plane-polarised light in opposite directions. (c) Use a chiral catalyst or enzyme (stereoselective synthesis); start from a natural chiral molecule (chiral pool); or resolve the racemate (chiral chromatography / diastereomeric salts).

(a) Explain what is meant by a chiral centre and describe how the two enantiomers differ. (b) Explain why the two enantiomers have different effects in the body. (c) Give two advantages of producing the single enantiomer rather than the racemate.
items.answer: (a) A carbon atom attached to four different groups; enantiomers are non-superimposable mirror images that rotate plane-polarised light in opposite directions. (b) Receptors and enzymes are chiral; only one enantiomer fits the binding site correctly (like a hand in a glove). (c) Smaller dose; fewer side effects; less waste; better regulatory approval / patent protection.
